entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Peter, commonly known as Peter of Tarentaise, emerged as a pivotal figure in the 12th-century ecclesiastical and political landscape of the western Alps. Born around 1102 in Saint-Maurice-de-Laq in the Dauphiné region, he abandoned a promising military career to join the burgeoning Cistercian Order at Bonnevaux Abbey in 1122. His rapid ascent within the order culminated in his election as Archbishop of Tarentaise in 1141, a position he held until his death in 1174. Peter's significance lies not only in his spiritual leadership but also in his tireless efforts as a peacemaker and papal legate amidst the complex feudal rivalries and the profound papal schism that defined his era.

Throughout his archiepiscopate, Peter dedicated himself to reforming the local clergy, promoting monastic discipline, and alleviating poverty. However, his most notable contributions were in the realm of diplomacy. He frequently mediated disputes between powerful regional lords, including Count Humbert III of Savoy and the Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa, earning a reputation for impartiality and wisdom. Crucially, Peter played an instrumental role during the protracted Papal Schism of 1159, advocating vigorously for Pope Alexander III against the anti-popes Victor IV and Paschal III. He undertook numerous diplomatic missions across France and the Holy Roman Empire, even participating in the Council of Tours in 1163, to solidify support for Alexander III.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Peter of Tarentaise was a significant regional figure whose tireless diplomatic efforts as an archbishop and papal legate helped stabilize the turbulent Alpine regions and contributed to the resolution of the Papal Schism of 1159, solidifying papal authority.
